subject: ELF – Engelsk läsförståelse
title: ELF – övningsprov 2
sourceSummary: Original practice items in the Högskoleprovet ELF format. This is not an officially released test.

stimulus.title: Text 1 – Paths nobody planned
stimulus.body:
Walk across almost any park or campus and you will find them: narrow strips of worn grass that cut a corner or link two buildings that the official paths do not connect. Planners call them desire lines, and for a long time they were treated as a nuisance. Fences went up, signs asked people to keep off the grass, and the worn strips were reseeded, only to reappear a few weeks later.

Some designers have learned to see them differently. A desire line, they argue, is a free survey: thousands of people voting with their feet on where a path ought to go. Rather than guessing in advance, a few universities and parks have deliberately left new areas unpaved for a season, then laid paths along the routes that walkers had already chosen.

The approach has limits. People take the shortest route, which is not always the safest one, and a path worn across a slope can speed up erosion. A desire line tells you where people want to go; it does not tell you whether they should. Still, the shift in attitude is telling. Instead of asking how to make people follow the plan, these designers ask how the plan can follow people.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the text?
choices: Fences and signs are the best way to protect the grass in parks
Planners should never lay paths before people have walked an area
Desire lines are mainly caused by careless walkers
Informal paths can show planners where paths are needed, although they should not always be followed
questions.explanation: The text moves from treating desire lines as a nuisance to using them as information, and then adds the limits of that approach. Option B ignores those limits ("never"), and the text does not blame careless walkers.

stimulus.title: Text 2 – Washing hands in Vienna
stimulus.body:
In the 1840s, the Vienna General Hospital ran two maternity clinics side by side. In one, women were delivered by doctors and medical students; in the other, by midwives. Year after year, far more mothers died of childbed fever (an infection after giving birth) in the doctors' clinic, and the difference was large enough that some women begged to be admitted to the other one.

Ignaz Semmelweis, a young doctor at the hospital, noticed that the doctors and medical students often came to the wards straight from performing autopsies. He suspected that they carried something from the bodies on their hands, and in 1847 he required everyone to wash in a solution of chlorinated lime before examining patients. Deaths in his clinic fell dramatically.

Yet many of his colleagues rejected the idea. Germ theory had not yet been established, so Semmelweis could not explain what, exactly, was being carried, and his conclusion implied that doctors themselves had been killing their patients. He also did little to win people over: he published his findings late and often answered criticism with anger.

He died in 1865, his work still largely ignored. Only in the following decades, as the role of microbes became clear, was he recognised as a pioneer. His story is often told as one of truth defeated by prejudice, but it is also a reminder that being right is rarely enough on its own.

questions.prompt: What did Semmelweis suspect was causing the higher death rate in the doctors' clinic?
choices: The doctors' clinic was more crowded than the other
The doctors used chlorinated lime in the wrong way
Doctors and students carried something from autopsies to the patients on their hands
The midwives were more experienced than the doctors
questions.explanation: Semmelweis noticed that doctors and students came to the wards straight from autopsies and suspected they carried something from the bodies on their hands. Chlorinated lime was his solution, not the cause.

stimulus.title: Text 3 – The rat tails of Hanoi
stimulus.body:
In 1902, the French colonial authorities in Hanoi faced a growing problem. A modern sewer system had been built under the city, and it had turned out to be an ideal home for rats. With plague a real danger, the authorities hired rat catchers and, when that proved too slow, offered residents a small reward for every rat they killed. To avoid having to handle dead rats, officials asked only for the tail as proof.

At first the scheme appeared to work, as thousands of tails were handed in. Soon, however, officials began to notice rats without tails running through the streets. Some hunters had realised that a living rat could go on breeding and produce more tails in the future, so they simply cut off the tail and let the animal go. There were even reports of people raising rats for the reward. The programme was eventually abandoned.

Economists sometimes call such outcomes perverse incentives: rewards that encourage the very behaviour they were meant to stop. A similar story about a reward for dead cobras in colonial India is often repeated, though historians have found little evidence that it actually happened. The Hanoi case, by contrast, is documented in the colonial authorities' own records, and it remains a useful warning to anyone who designs a reward: people respond to what is measured, not to what was intended.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the text?
choices: The story about cobras in India is better documented than the Hanoi case
Colonial authorities were unable to deal with disease
A reward can backfire if people can earn it without meeting the actual goal
Rats spread quickly in cities with modern sewers
questions.explanation: The Hanoi story is used to illustrate perverse incentives: the reward was paid for tails, and people found ways to earn it that did not reduce the number of rats. The text says the cobra story is the less reliable one.

stimulus.title: Text 4 – Half asleep
stimulus.body:
Sleep is a risky business for a wild animal. A sleeping creature cannot watch for predators, and an animal that lives in the water may not be able to breathe. Some species have found a remarkable solution: they let only half of the brain sleep at a time.

Dolphins are the best-known example. Recordings of their brain activity show that one hemisphere can enter deep sleep while the other stays awake, and that the two sides take turns. Meanwhile the animal keeps swimming slowly and surfaces to breathe, often with one eye open – the eye controlled by the waking half of the brain.

Birds can do something similar. In one well-known study of ducks resting in a row, the birds at the ends of the row slept with one eye open far more often than those in the middle, and the open eye was usually turned away from the group, towards the side from which danger was most likely to come. The ducks, in other words, seemed to adjust how much of the brain to keep awake depending on how exposed they were.

Humans cannot sleep like this, but researchers have found a faint echo of it. On the first night in an unfamiliar place, one half of the sleeper's brain tends to sleep less deeply than the other, which may help explain why people often sleep badly in a new hotel room.

questions.prompt: What is the text mainly about?
choices: Why dolphins need less sleep than other animals
How some animals can sleep with one half of the brain at a time
Why people sleep badly in hotels
How birds protect each other from predators
questions.explanation: The first paragraph introduces half-brain sleep, and the following ones give examples: dolphins, ducks and a faint human version. Hotels and birds are parts of the text, not its main subject.

stimulus.title: Text 5 – The lens that saved ships
stimulus.body:
For most of history, a lighthouse was only as useful as the fire or lamp at its top, and most of that light was wasted. It spread in every direction, upwards into the sky and downwards onto the rocks, while only a small part reached the ships it was meant to warn.

Curved mirrors helped, but the real breakthrough came in the 1820s from the French physicist Augustin Fresnel. A conventional lens large enough to gather a lighthouse's light would have been enormously thick and heavy, and much of the light would have been absorbed by the glass itself. Fresnel's insight was that the thick glass in the middle of a lens does almost nothing to focus the light; the work is done where the light passes through the lens's surfaces. He divided the curved surface into a series of concentric rings, each set at the correct angle, and placed them close together. The result did the work of a huge lens with a fraction of the glass.

The effect was dramatic. A light that had once been visible for a few miles could now be seen from more than twenty, and lighthouses along dangerous coasts were fitted with the new lenses within a few decades.

The same principle is still in use today, in places most people never notice: traffic lights, camera flashes and the thin plastic magnifiers sold as bookmarks all rely on Fresnel's rings.

questions.prompt: According to the text, what was the main problem with early lighthouses?
choices: They were often built in the wrong places
Their fires often went out in bad weather
Most of their light did not reach the ships
Their mirrors were too heavy to use
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says most of the light was wasted: it went up into the sky and down onto the rocks, and only a small part reached the ships.

The effect was dramatic. A light that had once been visible for a few miles could now be seen from more than twenty, and lighthouses along dangerous coasts were fitted with the new lenses within a few decades.

The same principle is still in use today, in places most people never notice: traffic lights, camera flashes and the thin plastic magnifiers sold as bookmarks all rely on Fresnel's rings.
